             Summary conclusions

This chapter has been concerned with the depiction of the people of South-
East Italy and their behaviour. The first section dealt with the indigenous
population. Although indigenous people governed the vast majority of the
territory of ancient Puglia and were  vitally important  clients for the
producers of Apulian red-figure, they were rarely depicted, appearing on
less than two per cent of all vases. Given that some red-figure workshops
were probably located in indigenous territory and it is likely that many
producers were from that population, it is perhaps strange that they were
not shown more  frequently.  Instead,  if  the  customers  did  identify
themselves with the figures on the vases, and it seems probable that they
did, it would seem that, for the most part, indigenous people were happy to
see themselves in the figures who wore Greek dress or were depicted
naked. Presumably, the content of the scenes was sufficiently positive, and
aligned with the values that burying communities wished to stress at the
funerals of their loved ones, that the costume did not matter. Moreover, it
is not necessarily the case that indigenous people wore their distinctive
costumes all the time. By the Fourth Century BC, they may have dressed
in the Greek mode most of the time, reserving the indigenous costume for
special occasions. It is not that indigenous identity had ceased to matter
but rather that it did not need to be stressed in every aspect of the funerary
practices, although the practices themselves would have been distinctive to
the local communities. Moreover, it is very possible that the dead would
have been attired in traditional costume for the funeral. In Central Puglia,
however, some people wished to have their ethnicity signalled in vase-
painting.31 This was usually done (in almost 85 per cent of cases) on
column-kraters, which served as the modern counterpart to the large vessel
that had always been the ceramic centerpiece of indigenous graves in the
area. The custom occurred throughout  the  history of Apulian vase-
painting, peaking in the Middle Apulian period before declining in the
Late Apulian. In the Late Apulian period, indigenous men were depicted
on a wider range of vessels but less frequently. The decline of the column-
krater may have played a part in this change but it would be unwise to
assume that the decrease in the number of indigenous scenes meant that
local identities were also in retreat. The depiction of indigenous men on
Apulian red-figure vases had only ever been a phenomenon of Central
Puglia but local identities continued to matter in Southern and Northern

154                            Chapter Five


Puglia throughout the Fourth Century and beyond. Presumably, what
changed  is  that  red-figure  vases were no  longer  seen  as such an
appropriate vehicle for the expression of Central Apulian identities as the
Fourth Century wore on.
   The second section dealt with vases depicting the honouring of the
dead. The theme could not be more apposite for vessels that were destined
to be put into graves. While it may not have been the intended function, at
the point of manufacture or acquisition by the original owners, of many of
the vases in the database, virtually all of them eventually made their way
into tombs. Of course, both producers and clients would have known about
local funerary practices, so presumably they would have been aware that
vessels may have been deposited in tombs at some future point. Vases
with naiskos scenes were different in that their iconography deliberately
referenced the honouring of the dead. It is, of course, possible that some
may have been used in everyday life, where their iconography may have
been interpreted as representing their owners’ piety towards the dead, and
especially their own ancestors, however,  it seems likely that most were
produced solely for the grave, where the focus would have been on the
figure of the deceased inside the monument. They were not, for the most
part, special commissions, although a few may have been, e.g. the vessels
showing indigenous men in the naiskoi and those showing actors, rather
they simply needed to align with the burying community’s values in terms
of how they commemorated the dead member of the community. Thus, it
was probably important that the gender of the person depicted on the vase
matched that of the deceased. Beyond that, the kind of values suggested by
the various accoutrements that accompanied the deceased in the naiskos
were pretty universal, though it may have been the case that some objects
were considered more pertinent to the deceased individual than others, e.g.
depicting a man with armour may have been considered  especially
appropriate for younger men.
   The main point of the iconography was to show that the deceased was
worthy of honour and would be remembered appropriately by the burying
community. Such scenes may have been reassuring  to the mourners
adjusting to the loss of an important member of the community and may
have been felt to have been reassuring to the dead. Certainly, in ancient
Greek literature, the dead cared about how they were remembered. In the
Odyssey (Book 11.50-80), Elpenor asks to be remembered, mourned, and
given a proper burial. Failure to fulfil these requests may result in his
bringing ill-fortune on the rest of Odysseus’ voyage. Presumably, similar
views obtained in South-East  Italy.  It was essential to bury the dead
properly, with the appropriate rituals and offerings, and to show that they

Celebrating Indigenous Life and Commemorating the Dead       155


were remembered. The vessels showing naiskos scenes, and, indeed, the
entire funerary  ritual, were devoted to addressing these concerns. No
doubt, a community risked supernatural sanctions if it failed to bury and
commemorate its dead properly. It would appear that these values were
particularly important to the indigenous community. Although none of the
vases with naiskos scenes is recorded, in RVAp and its Supplements, as
having come from a Greek cemetery, it would be unwise to assume that
these values applied solely to the indigenous community. Only 84 out of
1,235 vessels with naiskos scenes have a reliable find-spot noted in RVAp
and its Supplements, just 6.80 per cent of the total (1,235 vessels). The
provenance data are too partial and too imperfectly recorded to allow us to
be certain that naiskos scenes were exclusively associated with indigenous
people. After all, the kind of monument depicted on the vases had its
origins in Greek funerary monuments.
   The growing popularity of naiskos scenes over time is an interesting
phenomenon. It cannot reflect a greater interest in ensuring that the dead
were properly honoured. After all, more or less all of the Early and Middle
Apulian vessels in the sample were placed in graves in honour of the dead,
yet naiskos scenes were comparatively rare in these periods. Moreover,
scenes with stelai occur with reasonable frequency in the Early and Middle
Apulian periods, 3.75 per cent of Early Apulian vases feature a stele (60 of
1,599 vessels) as do 6.51 per cent of Middle Apulian vessels (171 of 2,625
vessels). While not all of these scenes were necessarily concerned with
honouring the dead, presumably some would have been. It is notable that
the percentage of vessels featuring stelai also increases in the Late Apulian
period, to 8.25 per cent (775 of 9,365 vessels). Presumably what changed
in the Late Apulian period was that there was a greater taste for the
commemoration  of  the  dead  to  be  explicitly  referenced on  vase-
iconography. This is reflected in the increase in the number and frequency
of both naiskos and stele scenes.
   Another  feature  of  the period  is  the  increase  in  the number  of
depictions of women inside naiskos. This could reflect a social change by
which women had become more prominent in society, perhaps as a result
of the growing importance of weaving as an economic activity.  It  is
difficult to explain the remarkable prosperity of indigenous communities
in the Fifth and Fourth Centuries BC but, to this day, the surfaces of the
sites are littered with loomweights, suggesting the weaving was practised
on a massive scale at this time.32 It is not unlikely that wool and/or textiles
were an important part of the indigenous economy in the pre-Roman era
(Whitehouse & Wilkins 1989). Weaving was strongly associated with
women in ancient Italy and a scene of weaving is preserved on one of the

156                            Chapter Five


so-called Daunian stelai from Northern Puglia (Manfredonia Museum, inv.
0699-0700; Nava 1980: 134, no 585 B, Tav. CLXIX). Alternatively, the
increased presence of women as the principal figures in naiskos scenes
may not reflect a major societal change so much as a transformation in the
social visibility of women, especially in the context of their own funerals.
Either  way, women  become  more  prominent  as  the  subjects  of
commemoration on Apulian vases in the late Fourth Century BC.

CHAPTER SIX

            CONCLUSIONS




The way in which the vast majority of the surviving Apulian red-figure
vases were recovered has resulted in the irretrievable loss of vital evidence
about the context in which they were used. Although we know that
virtually  all of them derive from tombs,  for most we do not have
information about the site at which they were found, the type of tomb in
which they were deposited, the gender, age, and social identity of the
deceased, whose  body/bodies  they  accompanied,  the  other  objects,
including the other Apulian red-figure vessels, with which they were
associated, where they were placed in the tomb, in relation to the corpse/s
and the other grave goods, or the  rituals associated with  their  final
deposition in the grave. Nothing can compensate for this loss.
   One of the corollaries of the excavation history of this type of pottery
has been the tendency to approach vases as objets d’art rather than as
contextualised archaeological artefacts. The recovery of vases has been
motivated by the tastes of collectors and the commercial interests of
international auction houses. Originally, scholars of Apulian pottery were
either collectors themselves or served  their aims by cataloguing and
publishing their collections. For modern scholars, viewing Apulian red-
figure through an art-historical lens is partly a matter of locating their
research within the history of the scholarship and partly a result of force
majeure – other approaches that are routinely applied to ancient artefacts
are closed to such decontextualised material. The result has been that
scholars have tended to focus on stylistic issues and small groups of vases,
united by the content of their iconography rather than the context of their
usage.
   The importance and excellence of the previous scholarship cannot be
questioned. It would not have been possible to attempt this book without
the painstaking work of Trendall and Cambitoglou in cataloguing so many
Apulian vases, but the aim in this volume has been to attempt a somewhat
different approach to the study of the material. While the vases cannot be
recontextualised in terms of their original provenance information, the
sample size means that the material can be viewed in a wider context, that

158                            Chapter Six


of production. This allowed both the production of individual vase forms
and particular iconographic trends to be seen within the context of that part
of the original output of the industry that eventually found its way into
tombs.
   The sample, because of its sheer size, can be accepted as a reliable
analogue of the material that was placed in tombs, even though RVAp and
its Supplements were not, and were never, intended to be a comprehensive
corpus of all surviving Apulian red-figure vases. However, we cannot be
so certain that it would be so reliable in terms of mimicking the entire
output of the industry. It is possible that some vase forms or certain types
of iconography were deemed much more suitable for the grave than others.
If this were the case, it would skew the sample, so that it would not be
representative of the industry as a whole.
   The entirety of the production and the relative importance of different
vase forms in terms of the surviving output of the industry was the subject
of Chapter Two. The fact that the overall output expanded massively in the
Late Apulian phase has long been known but documenting the extent of
the growth accurately revealed that nearly 70 per cent of all surviving
Apulian vessels date from the final phase of production (Table 1). This
undoubtedly reflects changing social customs and burial practices, with
more vessels being placed in graves, red-figure vases being available for
use in the graves of a wider cross-section of the population, and an overall
increase in the total number of burials. Nonetheless, that there was a real
growth in output seems impossible to deny.
   Some of the forms considered to be most characteristic of Apulian red-
figure were revealed to be either of minor importance in numerical terms,
e.g. the nestoris, or were only truly significant in the Late Apulian phase,
e.g. the patera and the volute-krater. The nestoris and the patera are the
two forms that do not derive from the repertoire of Greek pottery, while
the volute-krater  is perhaps the shape that  first comes to mind when
thinking of Apulian red-figure. However, the most commonly surviving
forms are the oenochoe, the bell-krater, and the pelike, none of which
would be considered to be especially characteristic of Apulian red-figure.
   The dominance of forms related to the storage, preparation, serving,
and drinking of wine was also striking. More than 70 per cent of all
vessels were connected to wine. It is debatable as to whether this reflects
the actual output of the industry or whether the importance of wine is
exaggerated by the context of the funerary banquet. It is possible that the
centrality of wine in funerary ritual meant that vessels connected with
wine were over-represented in the sample. In addition to playing an
essential  part in the funerary banquet, wine may have carried other

Conclusions                         159


connotations that were symbolically important in ancient South-East Italy.
These may have included the display of social status and connectedness, in
terms of having access to good quality wine, possibly of Greek origin or at
least purporting to be, and also the worship of Dionysos, a god associated
with wine, the theatre, and death and  rebirth. Although a very high
percentage of Apulian vessels comes from the graves of the indigenous
population, whose burial practices encouraged the deposition of objects in
the grave, Dionysos is not one of the Greek gods whose worship is attested
in the Messapic inscriptions (Parlangèli 1960 ; Santoro 1982 ; 1984).
Nevertheless,  it  is  clear  that  the  indigenous  population knew who
Dionysos was and what he represented. The evidence of vase-painting
alone  is enough  to  demonstrate  his  importance  to  the  indigenous
population.
    Interestingly, while no major forms died out entirely across the history
of production, there were plenty that only came to prominence in the Late
Apulian phase. These include some very popular forms, such as the
kantharos, the lekanis, and the plate. More than 90 per cent of examples of
each of these shapes, as well as those of the somewhat less common askos,
alabastron, epichysis, and pyxis, date to the Late Apulian period. Most of
these shapes are comparatively small and often they are adorned with
highly generic decoration. In the context of the massive expansion of the
output of the industry, these forms and their characteristic decoration, look
almost like the results of mass production, as complexity and originality
were  sacrificed  to  the  speed  of  production. However,   it must  be
remembered  that  volute-kraters, which were  often  very  large,  and,
therefore, challenging to make, as well as being adorned with highly
original multi-figure compositions, only really come to the fore in the
same period; more than 80 per cent of all volute-kraters date to the Late
Apulian phase. The pattern of production is, therefore, more variegated
than it superficially appears.
   Generic decoration is highly characteristic of Apulian red-figure and
contributes to giving it something of a bad name among connoisseurs of
ancient pottery. Although most of the previous scholarship on Apulian
red-figure has focused on the iconography, the most generic scenes have
attracted less attention than their overall importance in the production
suggests that they deserve. Chapter Three focussed on the two most
common types of generic decoration, namely the depiction of draped
youths and portrait heads.
   Draped youths are only to be found on the reverses of larger vessels.
The popularity of such scenes is striking as more than 20 per cent of all
vases have draped youths on their reverses. Although vessels may show

160                            Chapter Six


any number from one  to  four  youths, two  is  the most common
composition, with more than 80 per cent of all examples following this
standard. Two vessel forms, both kraters, are dominated by this type of
decoration on the reverse. Over 75 per cent of bell-kraters and more than
70 per cent of column-kraters feature draped youths on their reverses.
Draped youths are far less common on the other krater forms. They appear
with some regularity, however, on amphorae, nestorides, and pelikai but
are otherwise comparatively rare. Another notable pattern that emerges
with regard to scenes of draped youths is the decline in their popularity
through time. Just over a quarter of all scenes of draped youths date to the
Late Apulian period, even though nearly 70 per cent of all vases belong to
that phase (Table 2).
   Although scenes of draped youths are highly standardised, they are
nothing like as repetitive as the depictions of heads. More than 35 per cent
of all vessels had a head portrait, with more than 30 per cent having one
that occupied a main field of decoration. These data are made all the more
remarkable by the fact that head scenes are, by and large, a Late Apulian
feature. Almost 98 per cent of all such scenes date to that phase (Tables 3
and 4). Unlike the draped youths, head scenes occur on a very wide range
of forms, being especially popular on kantharoi, lekanides, plates, pyxides,
and various cup forms. Although heads are especially prominent on small
forms that emerge in the Late Apulian period, they are by no means
limited to these forms. Moreover, heads are not especially popular on all
Late Apulian morphological newcomers. For instance, less than four per
cent of epichysides feature a head scene. Another striking factor of these
scenes is the prevalence of depictions of female heads. In roughly 98 per
cent of cases, the head is female. Female heads reign supreme regardless
of whether the vessel form was particularly associated with women or not.
As there must have been little difference in the time and ability required to
paint a female head as opposed to a male, one can only conclude that the
dominance of female heads was a deliberate choice and a matter of local
taste.
   The more complex iconography, that has long captured the attention of
connoisseurs and scholars, was the topic of Chapters Four and Five.
Chapter Four dealt with scenes of myth and drama, as well as more
generic depictions of the gods. Although there can be  little doubt that
productions of Greek tragedies influenced the iconography of Apulian
vases, it is difficult to be sure that the images of myth on vases depict
theatrical performances. While the choice of myths shown would appear to
have been strongly indebted to the productions of the plays of Euripides,
Sophocles and others that were staged in South-East Italy in the Fourth

Conclusions                         161


Century BC, the fact that the figures do not wear theatrical masks and
costumes, the lack of the chorus, and the absence of images of the stage
itself, perhaps suggests that the scenes were intended to show the myths
themselves and not actors telling the story of the myth. However, in the
case of comic performances, the so-called phlyax vases, it is clear that the
vases were dealing with theatrical subject matter.
   Unless scenes showing comic actors were much more popular in
domestic contexts and were largely deemed unsuitable for the grave, it is
safe to say that they were only ever a tiny part of the output of the
industry, occurring on less than half of one per cent of all vases. Even at
their peak, in the Early Apulian period (Table 5), they account for less than
two and a half per cent of the total of vases in the database. That said,
when phlyakes are depicted, they mostly occur on the obverse of the
vessels in question, giving the subject matter a degree of prominence. The
association between phlyax scenes and bell-kraters is very pronounced,
with over 50 per cent of all phlyax scenes occurring on examples of the
form. There is also an association, albeit somewhat less strong, with calyx-
kraters and oenochoai. Otherwise such scenes appear on just one or two
occasions on  other vase forms.  Generally,  the  data  reveal a  strong
association between phlyax scenes and vessels connected with the mixing
and serving of wine. This suggests a link between scenes of comic
performance and Dionysos, the god of wine and theatre.
   Scenes of mythology, which potentially also include scenes from
Greek tragedy, are especially valued by collectors and have been a fertile
ground for iconographic studies. Once again, the attention that vases
bearing such scenes have attracted outweighs their numerical significance
in terms of the entire output of the industry; just five per cent of all
Apulian vases show a mythological scene. Mythology was most important
as a source of inspiration for vase-painters in the Early and, especially,
Middle Apulian phases (Table 6). With the rise of small vessels dominated
by generic images in the Late Apulian period, so mythological scenes
declined  in importance  in  relative terms. However, they continue to
occupy the obverses of many of the largest and most striking vases, which
perhaps gave the scenes a greater prominence, especially in the context of
the funeral.
   Mythological scenes are especially popular on calyx-kraters, where
more than 35 per cent of all such vessels had some mythological subject
matter. They are also prominent on volute-kraters, despite the fact that the
form enjoys its greatest popularity in the Late Apulian phase. Almost half
of all mythological scenes occur on wine-mixing vessels.

162                            Chapter Six


   In terms of content, the most popular subjects are: stories from the
Trojan War, Amazonomachy scenes, and the myths of Herakles. No other
subjects account for more than five per cent of all mythological scenes.
While Amazonomachy scenes are sometimes shown in secondary zones of
decoration, the more elaborate stories of the Trojan War and of Herakles
generally occur on the principal decorative fields on the obverses of vases.
   Another very notable feature of the mythological subjects that appear
on Apulian vases is their sheer variety. There are numerous myths that
appear on only one or two occasions. Moreover,  there  is a  certain
fascination with obscure stories.
   Given that most of the vases in the sample would have been deposited
in indigenous graves, it would appear that there was a deep knowledge of
and interest in Greek mythology among the indigenous communities, or at
least among the social élites, i.e. those buried with the largest and most
elaborately decorated vases. That said, vases with mythological scenes
also appear to have been popular among the Greeks. Out of 134 vessels
with mythological scenes with reliable find-spots recorded in RVAp and its
Supplements, 31, or 23.13 per cent, come from Taranto, v. Notes 22 and
24.
   The gods also appear on Apulian vases in more generic portrayals and
in  association  with  humans,  indicating  their  favour  of  particular
individuals and activities. Including mythological scenes, gods appear on
nearly forty per cent of all surviving vases and the popularity of images of
the gods  is fairly consistent over time (Table 7). Generally, the gods
appeared on the obverses of vases, perhaps indicating their importance, or,
at least, that the reverses were more commonly given over to highly
generic decoration.
   The gods were much more common on some forms than others. They
were especially well represented on calyx-kraters, dinoi, lebetes gamikoi,
and situlae but decidedly rare on amphorae and hydriai, suggesting that
these latter forms were more commonly painted with scenes of the human
world.
   Eros was the most commonly depicted god and his popularity grew
over time. Dionysos and his entourage of satyrs and silens, etc., were also
very popular, especially in the Early and Middle Apulian phases. In the
Late Apulian phase, the popularity of Dionysian themes declined and was
superseded by themes  of love and  victory. Nike,  too,  increased  in
popularity in the Late Apulian phase and the victors that she celebrated
were often successful in romantic endeavours rather than sport or war.
None of the other gods was depicted particularly often.

Conclusions                         163


   The  association  of  particular  vase  forms  with  certain  gods  is
noteworthy. Eros dominates divine imagery on  alabastra, cup forms,
epichysides, lebetes gamikoi, and paterae to a remarkable degree. The
association  of  the  lebes gamikos with  the god  of  love  is perhaps
unremarkable but the extent of Eros’ domination of its iconography is.
More than 95 per cent of all divine scenes that appear on lebetes gamikoi
show Eros.
   Dionysos and his entourage are especially common on bell-kraters,
calyx-kraters, column-kraters, dinoi, and situlae, all forms connected with
the preparation of wine. However, the association of Dionysian figures
with particular forms is never as strong as the sway Eros holds over the
forms that he dominates.
   Dionysos was the god of wine, which fits with the function of the vase
forms that he dominates. His mythology also had connotations of death
and rebirth that were apt for vessels that were eventually deposited in
graves. It is notable, however, that in the Late Apulian phase, when the
output of the Apulian industry was  at  its  greatest, Eros became the
dominant god.  It would seem that, by that time, the living wished to
remember their dead as favoured by the god of love and desire and perhaps
hoped that his favour would endure after death.
   Chapter Five concerned  itself with  depictions  of  the indigenous
population and the so-called naiskos scenes that show the honouring of the
dead inside architectural funerary monuments. As with other distinctive
aspects  of  the iconography  of Apulian  red-figure, both  topics have
captured  the  imagination  of  earlier  scholars. On  the  scenes  of  the
indigenous population, it is the men who stand out because they wear the
striking local costume. Unlike their counterparts on Campanian vessels,
the women depicted on scenes of indigenous  life on Apulian vases
generally wear Greek dress (Herring 2009b).
   Although scenes of indigenous life have attracted considerable interest
in the past, vessels decorated in this way account for less than two per cent
of all Apulian vases. As was the case with mythological subjects, the level
of interest in indigenous life was high, in relative terms, in the Early
Apulian phase and peaked in the Middle Apulian (Table 8). Indigenous
scenes only occur on a limited number of forms and the column-krater was
overwhelmingly the most popular form for  this type of iconography.
Almost 85 per cent of all indigenous scenes occurred on column-kraters.
In the Early and Middle Apulian phases, that dominance was around 95
per cent. The provenance data, for all their limitations, strongly suggest
that scenes of indigenous life appear on vessels destined for use in the
tombs of Central Puglia, v. Note 28. It is quite likely that they were also

164                            Chapter Six


made in the same area, as the painters clearly knew the tastes of their
clients. The column-krater had long been important in Central Puglia,
although the form was quite rare in Athenian pottery (v., e.g., Burn 2000:
134). The shape had entered the repertoire of indigenous ceramics in the
region by  the  late  Sixth Century BC (Herring 2000: 101-104) and
Carpenter (2018: 69) has stressed its relationship to earlier local pottery
forms. Furthermore, there was a long established tradition in South-East
Italy to place a large vessel, alongside at least one smaller one, in adult
graves. Apulian red-figure column-kraters were considered highly suitable
for this role in the Fourth Century BC, as, indeed, were other wine-mixing
forms.
   Although column-kraters dominated, indigenous people appeared quite
frequently on nestorides. Moreover, the form, and its relatives in other
ceramic  traditions, was  quite commonly  depicted on  column-kraters
showing  indigenous  life;  such  vessels were  only  ever shown  with
indigenous people. This suggests a strong link between the form, which,
after  all, derived from indigenous ceramic traditions (Colivicchi 2014:
215-216, fig. 10.1), and the expression of indigenous identity. There is
other evidence to suggest that the nestoris was particularly associated with
women (Herring 2018: 62-64).
   All in all, the vessels depicting the non-Greek population of South-East
Italy were almost certainly made for the people of Central Puglia for use in
their tombs. The vases were deposited in accordance with long established
practice. They  depicted  indigenous men  dressed  in  their  traditional
costume in a broadly positive  light, albeit in versions of scenes that
normally feature men dressed in Greek attire or depicted in a state of
heroic nudity.  It would seem that these stock images chimed with the
values that the burying community wanted to affirm about their deceased
loved ones. However, they had been crucially adapted to communicate a
powerful message about indigenous  identity. Why  it seems  to have
become less important to express that message in the later Fourth Century
is very  difficult to answer, as the indigenous peoples of South-East
remained strongly independent of each other and of the Italiote population
until the Roman conquest in the 270s BC.
   Scenes showing the honouring of the dead inside naiskoi were also
popular with the indigenous population. Naiskos scenes occur on roughly
nine per cent of all vases. They are at their most popular in the Late
Apulian period (Table 9), when close to 12 per cent of vessels show such
scenes. This type of iconography  is  virtually unknown  in the Early
Apulian phase.

Conclusions                         165


   The Late Apulian period is marked by a massive increase in the output
of the industry. The period sees the emergence of many smaller forms and
a very  strong tendency towards  generic  decoration,  especially head
portraits. The volute-krater comes to prominence at the same time. While
its trajectory of production puts the volute-krater in the same category as
many of the new forms, its average size, complex features, including the
extravagant handles and use of plastic additions, and elaborate decoration
run counter to the prevailing trends. The monumental character of many
volute-kraters strongly suggests that they were made for tombs. Their
iconography supports this.
   Naiskos scenes are especially common on volute-kraters, with half of
all such scenes occurring on the form. Trendall considered the volute-
krater to be “the most characteristic of all Apulian shapes” (RFVSIS: 9).
Given that close to 80 per cent of all volute-kraters had a naiskos scene,
one could, therefore, reasonably suggest that naiskos scenes are highly
characteristic of Apulian red-figure, especially as naiskos scenes usually
occupied the obverses of the vases that they adorned. Naiskos scenes were
also popular on amphorae, barrel-amphorae, hydriai, and loutrophoroi.
Otherwise, they make only occasional appearances on a few other forms.
   Often the entire iconography of vases with naiskos scenes was devoted
to the honouring of the dead. This was for one of three reasons: first,
because the vessel had only a single field of decoration, as in the case of
the hydriai; second, because the vessel had a naiskos scene on both of its
sides; or third, because it had a naiskos scene on the obverse and a stele
scene on the reverse. Over five per cent of vessels had the honouring of the
dead as the principal theme of the iconography.
   Although some naiskos scenes featured objects, divine figures, or more
than one individual inside the monument, most, almost 90 per cent of
examples, have a single figure as the principal honorand. Although men
dominate, women are, by no means, unrepresented in this role. Indeed, the
ratio of men to women is close to 60:40 and, over time, women become
more prominent, as naiskos scenes become more common.
  On some vase forms, men are clearly in the ascendency, notably
volute-kraters, where men account for close to 80 per cent of the total, and
amphorae, where they make up nearly 70 per cent of principal figures. On
other forms, including hydriai, loutrophoroi, barrel-amphorae and pelikai,
women are more prominent. In the case of hydriai, the association with
women is close to exclusive; almost 98 per cent of principal figures in
naiskoi on hydriai are female.
   Although naiskos scenes were,  in some ways,  quite  generic, the
iconography was such that it could be seen as relevant to the individuals

166                            Chapter Six


with whom the vases were to be buried. The normal configuration showed
a man or woman in the monument with a number of objects that, in some
way, characterised them. Such objects might include armour for men, who
were portrayed as warriors. However, other men were represented by
artefacts connected with the cultured lifestyle, such as vases, lyres, etc. For
women, vessels, jewellery, and objects associated with adornment were
prominent. Both women and men could be attended in the naiskos, by
servants, indicating a leisured lifestyle. The presence of servants has the
possible implication that this privileged lifestyle would be maintained in
the afterlife. On each side of the naiskos, mourners are depicted, carrying
an array of objects, usually vases and fillets, to offer to the dead. Any
number between two and six mourners  is typical. Sometimes a god,
usually Eros, Nike,  or, occasionally, Hermes as the guider of souls,
appears with the mourners to indicate that the deceased had, and perhaps
would continue to enjoy, the favour of the gods.
  No doubt, the vases with the naiskos scenes were used at the funerary
banquet with  the  figure  in  the monument being  identified with  the
deceased  and  the  depictions  of  mourners  standing  for  the  actual
participants at the funeral. Simultaneously, the vase honoured the dead in
the present and promised a future in which that commemoration would
continue. The burying community, thereby, reassured itself, and perhaps
the deceased also, that the dead person was worthy of honour and that
community had performed, and would continue to fulfill, the duties that
were owed to the dead.
   The death of a member of a community was a time of grief and of
social  stress, as positions and relationships in society had to be  re-
evaluated. This was perhaps especially true when the deceased was a
prominent member  of  the  community,  as  those who  received  the
monumental volute-kraters probably were. The funeral played a significant
role in easing those social stresses, as the dead was honoured with the
appropriate  rituals  to  ensure  that  they  took  their  place among  the
community’s respected ancestors, satisfied that they had been sufficiently
respected by the community at large. It would seem that these notions
were of particular importance in South-East  Italy in the  later Fourth
Century BC.
   The importance of honouring the dead is one of a number of trends
evident in the Late Apulian period. Another was the massive increase in
the output of the industry. This itself suggests that more vases were being
placed in tombs, which  is complementary to the growing  interest in
honouring the dead. It may also suggest that a greater cross-section of the
community was able to access red-figure vases to place in the tombs of

Conclusions                         167


their loved ones. This may indicate that there was a desire to emulate the
behaviour of the social élite in terms of the objects that they put in the
graves of their family members. It may be the case that the production of
smaller vases, with highly generic decoration, was able to fulfill the desire
of members of other social groups to have red-figure vases put in their
tombs. In turn, this may have fuelled the growth in output of the industry.
At the same time, perhaps to reaffirm the difference between them and
other members of the community, the  élites may have increased the
lavishness of the funerary banquets and, consequently, the number of
vessels being placed in the tombs of their loved ones, as an illustration of
the deceased’s, and by extension their own, social capital and/or material
wealth. To mark  the  distinction  further,  they  deposited  elaborately
decorated and monumental vases, whose iconography could be seen to
refer to the life of the dead and the piety of the living.
   Other Late Apulian trends point to an increased visibility of women
both in terms of their prominence on naiskos scenes but also on generic
scenes, where female heads adorn so many vases. The growing popularity
of Eros in the same period may be possibly linked to an increasing
feminisation of the output of the industry. It may be that female graves
were receiving red-figure vases in increasing numbers in the late Fourth
Century and  that  this  partly drove the growth  in output. We might
speculate that in earlier periods, when vases were perhaps more likely to
be  deposited  in  the  graves  of men,  Dionysian themes were more
prominent. That said, it was not only women who were linked to Eros in
the Late Apulian period, men too were being characterised in death as
having been successful in arts of love and  it was perhaps hoped, or
anticipated, that the god’s favour would continue in the afterlife. This is
evidenced by many naiskos scenes, which depict a man as the principal
figure in the naiskos and also feature a scene with Eros in a secondary
location, e.g. the volute-krater (Naples 2022, inv. 82361) attributed to the
Bitonto Group (RVAp II, 28/287, pl. 372, 1-2).
   Ultimately, virtually all of the vases in the sample were deposited in
graves and were, therefore, used to honour the dead. While this was not
the original function of many vases, it was a typical part of a vessel’s “life
history”. No doubt, this was something of which both producers and
consumers were aware. That does not mean to say that in designing either
the shape or the iconography that producers always had one eye on the
grave. Rather, it might imply that when selecting vessels for deposition
with  the  dead,  the  burying  community  took  the  following  into
consideration: the requirements of the funerary rituals, and, especially, the
importance of wine consumption  at the banquet; established funerary

168                            Chapter Six


customs,  like making a  large vessel  the centrepiece of  the ceramic
assemblage in adult graves for the indigenous population; and the capacity
of the iconography to be considered relevant to the context of the burial
and the social identity of the deceased. As much of the iconography was
fairly standardised and emphasised values, such as piety, athleticism,
military prowess, beauty, success, and desirability, that could easily be
applied to much of the population, especially in a context where the
identity being celebrated was idealised and, perhaps sometimes, even
fictionalised. In other words, not all men necessarily needed to have had
successful military careers in real life in order to have been characterised
as warriors in the context of the funeral. This could be achieved not only
through the images on vase-painting but also by the inclusion of actual
pieces of weaponry and armour in the goods that accompanied them in the
grave. Similarly, not all women would have been beautiful or desirable but
the idealised social persona defined them as such. What mattered was how
the community wished to see the dead and perhaps how the dead wished
themselves to be remembered.
   For most Apulian vases, the loss of their provenance, with all the
myriad of associations that each vessel would have had, has forever
diminished their archaeological value. The purpose of this book has been
to  recontextualise  Apulian  red-figure  vases,  not  in  terms  of  their
provenance or precise context, but in terms of their place within the
totality of the output of the industry (or at least that part of it that made its
way into tombs). By doing so, it has been possible to map patterns in the
production of different vase forms and in the iconographic choices made
by vase-painters and changes in these patterns over time. Ultimately, these
patterns reflect the tastes and values of the consumers, and, particularly,
their requirements when burying their loved ones. This allows us to re-
imagine Apulian  red-figure  vases,  not  just  as  aesthetically  pleasing
artworks from a distant ancient past, but as objects that were used by real
people as active components in the remembrance of their dead.

1 Although South Italian tribes were referred to by both Herodotos and Thucydides,
most of  the sources  that deal with  the  region, including Diodorus  Siculus,
Pausanias, and Strabo, were writing long after the events that they describe, which
adds a further level of complexity when seeking to extrapolate evidence for
indigenous society from their narratives.
2 In addition to Rome becoming an important player in South-East Italian politics
in the Fourth and early Third Centuries BC, Oscan-speaking groups, including the
Samnites, from South-Central and South-West Italy also made encroachments into
Puglia. These mostly affected Central and Northern Puglia. For example, Diodorus
Siculus (20.80) mentions that the Romans besieged Silvium (Botromagno, near
modern Gravina), which had been garrisoned by the Samnites.
3 Tarentum had sought, not altogether successfully, to impose its hegemony over
the Greek communities of Southern Italy by taking over the leadership of the
Italiote League from Kroton in the early Fourth Century. By the second half of the
Fourth Century, Tarentum was increasingly reliant on foreign leaders and troops to
counter the ongoing  threat from the various groups  rivalling  for control of
Southern Italy. Strabo 6.3.4 lists the following Tarentine champions: Archidamus
III of Sparta, Alexander I of Molossia, Cleonymus of Sparta, and Pyrrhus of
Epirus.
4 Herakleia was a joint foundation between Tarentum and Thurii, itself an Athenian
foundation, located close to Sybaris. It was established in the vicinity of the earlier
settlement at Siris, which had been destroyed in the mid-Sixth Century BC. The
remains of Siris/Herakleia are to be found near modern Policoro.
